title: The Rise of the Fraud Economy
author: Christian Parenti
content:
![The Rise of the Fraud
Economy](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/Screenshot-2026-08-10-at-6.59.26
---AM.png)

> _How to Rule the World: An Education in Power at Stanford University_  
>  By Theo Baker  
> Penguin, 337 pages, $32

Fraud is an ancient practice, but these days its prevalence and scale seems to
be increasing. The latest evidence for this comes from _How to Rule the World_
, by the recent Stanford graduate Theo Baker. At one level the book is about
how Baker, as a college freshman working for the student newspaper _The_
_Stanford Daily_ , got the president of his university fired for having
perpetrated scientific fraud over at least a decade and a half. At another
level, the book offers an ethnographic account of the culture of fraud that
prevails not just at Stanford but across elite American institutions.

The culture of fraud at Stanford, in Baker's account, is as ubiquitous as soot
in a nineteenth-century industrial city: on every surface, in every crevice,
floating in the air you breathe. An early hint of the problem appears in the
"war on fun" that has stripped the soul out of student life. Parties, Baker
tells us, are very rare. Fraternity parties seem to happen only one at a time,
and like every other party, require approval by the university's official
Party Review Committee. Applications must be submitted by Tuesday if your
party is to occur on the weekend. Before entering the festivities, Baker
recalls, partygoers had to first recite and agree to a consent policy,
followed by a land acknowledgment. (In an apparent concession to the "vibe
shift," Stanford dropped the land acknowledgement in October 2025.)

Baker passes no judgment on these rituals, but a picture emerges of students
who draw ethical and political conclusions that are the opposite of what is
intended. Many who attend these fraternity parties no doubt think the land
acknowledgment is ridiculous. When they recite it, they are in effect spouting
lies mandated by university administrators. Regardless of what the
administrators think is going on, the real lesson--lie to get ahead--is
received.
